title: Sensor-Based Measurement of Fear Avoidance and Movement Patterns of Healthy Individuals with Mechanically Induced Lower Back Pain during Movement Tasks: Study Protocol for an Experimental Non-Interventional Study
summary:
Background:
Chronic low back pain is very common and can be both physically limiting and psychologically stressful. An important factor here is what is known as fear avoidance. This means that people avoid certain movements or activities for fear of pain—which can actually make the symptoms worse in the long run. Previous research shows that pain, physical activity, stress, and fear avoidance are interrelated. Interestingly, fear avoidance also occurs in people who are not currently experiencing any pain. However, what has not yet been thoroughly investigated is how fear avoidance and physical stress responses interact and how they influence movement patterns when back pain is artificially induced.

Methods:
We want to study 76 participants who are not currently experiencing pain (20 in phase 1, 56 in phase 2). All participants will perform specified everyday movement tasks, for example, picking up something from the floor, once without and once with a vest that artificially induces back pain. All participants will undergo both conditions, with and without simulated pain.
The movements are recorded using two modern measurement systems: a wearable sensor system (Xsens) and a new radar-based motion capture system. In addition, we measure physical stress responses, such as the stress hormone cortisol in saliva or heart rate variability. We also ask participants about their perceived stress, pain, and fear avoidance. In phase 1, we also conduct interviews to find out how well the experimental setup works and how acceptable the pain simulator is to participants.

Results (expected):
In phase 1, we check whether the new back pain simulator and the motion measurement systems used work well and are accepted by the participants. In phase 2, we investigate how artificially induced back pain affects self-reported pain, motion parameters, and stress responses. We also analyze the influence of anxiety avoidance on these factors.
We expect that the experimental setup will be easy to implement and will be well received. We also expect that participants, when wearing the back pain simulator, will report more pain, have reduced mobility, and show stronger stress responses than without the back pain simulator. We assume that people with more pronounced fear avoidance will also react more sensitively to the pain conditions—for example, with reduced mobility or increased stress.

Discussion:
This study design enables us, for the first time, to examine more closely under controlled conditions how pain, fear avoidance, stress, and movement interact in otherwise healthy individuals. Our goal is to better understand how psychological and physical processes interact, which play an important role in chronic back pain. In the long term, this knowledge could help develop new approaches to preventing or treating back pain.
conditions: Mechanically Induced Primary Lower Back Pain

interventions.name: Participants will perform standardized movement tasks (Back Performance Scale, Sit-To-Stand-Test) first with and then without wearing a back pain simulator in a crossover design.
Participants will perform standardized movement tasks (Back Performance Scale, Sit-To-Stand-Test) first without and then with wearing a back pain simulator in a crossover design.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1)	Sufficient knowledge of German (native speaker or C2 level)
2)	Body mass index (BMI) between ≥ 18 and ≤ 25 (due to the limited size range of the back pain simulator and Xsens suit)
3)	Body height ≥ 155 cm (setup requirement for back pain simulator and Xsens suit) 
4)	Good physical and mental health state (see exclusion criteria)
Exclusion criteria:
1)	Chronic back pain 
2)	Depression (exceed cut-off score for clinically relevant depression symptoms of 22 on the General Depression Scale (Allgemeine Depressionsskala; ADS-L;  Hautzinger, 2012)
3)	Serious diseases or conditions (e.g. cancer, severe epilepsy, acute psychosis); serious psychological disorders will be screened via the Web Screening Questionnaire for Common Mental Disorders (WSQ; Donkers et al., 2009)
4)	Acute infectious diseases (e.g. HIV/AIDS)
5)	Current pregnancy
6)	Acute herniation (e.g. spinal disc herniation)
7)	Acute back pain (ranging on a scale from 0 = no pain to 10 = worst imaginable pain between ≥ 5 and ≤ 10)
8)	Acute muscle and/or skeletal pain interfering with daily activities
9)	Diseases of the nerve roots and spine injuries
10)	Osteoporosis of the spine or back
11)	Surgery on or near the spine
12)	Diabetes mellitus (back pain simulator requirement, inter alia because of associated skin and soft tissue changes and higher risk of skin infections; e.g. Gkogkolou & Böhm, 2014)

References: 
Hautzinger M. Allgemeine Depressionsskala: ADS; Manual. Hogrefe; 2012.
Donker T, van Straten A, Marks IM, Cuijpers P, others. A brief Web-based screening questionnaire for common mental disorders: development and validation. J Med Internet Res. 2009;11(3):e1134.
Gkogkolou P, Böhm M. Skin disorders in diabetes mellitus. JDDG J Dtsch Dermatol Ges. 2014;12(10):847–64.
